title: How Bitcoin Mining Actually Works (Beginner Guide: Blocks, Hashes, Difficulty and Costs)
intro: A plain-English guide to how Bitcoin mining works: what a block is, what miners are really doing, why difficulty exists, how rewards work, and what costs and risks sit behind it. Educational only, with no promises of returns.
sources: Forklog: What is a digital miner

scenes.narration: If you have ever wondered how Bitcoin mining actually works, this video explains it from the ground up, with no hype and no promises. By the end, you will know what a block is, what miners are really doing, why difficulty exists, how rewards work, and what costs and risks sit behind it all.

items: Compete to add the next block

scenes.narration: Bitcoin miners compete to add the next block of transactions to the blockchain. The winner earns the block reward, which is the block subsidy plus transaction fees.
The protocol aims for one new block roughly every ten minutes on average. Mining is how the network decides who adds each one, and it does that using something called proof of work.
Each block stores the hash of the previous block's header. That is what links the blocks together into a chain.

Miners do not hash the whole block. Only the 80 byte block header goes through proof of work. That header holds the previous block's hash, the merkle root of the block's transactions, and a field called the nonce.

scenes.text: The nonce is easy to change
scenes.narration: The nonce is easy to modify. That matters, because it lets a miner change one small value and try a new hash, again and again.

Bitcoin mining uses SHA-256 hashing. Miners search for a block header hash that does not exceed a certain value, called the network target. It is not a puzzle you solve with clever maths. It is a search. If the hash is too high, the miner changes the nonce and tries again.
The lower the target, the rarer a winning hash is, so more attempts are needed on average.
The number of attempts a miner makes each second is called hashrate. One terahash per second, written T H slash S, means one trillion hashes every second.
If more miners join, do blocks come faster? Not for long. Difficulty is recalculated every 2,016 blocks, about two weeks, to keep block time near ten minutes.

visual.caption: the most it can move at once

scenes.narration: At each adjustment, difficulty can rise by as much as 300 percent, or fall by as much as 75 percent. So it can move in both directions.
That is why more miners does not simply mean faster blocks. The network adjusts the difficulty to keep the pace steady.

scenes.text: Hard to find, easy to check

items: Checking its proof of work: cheap

scenes.narration: Finding a valid block is computationally hard, but checking it is cheap. Other nodes can verify a block's proof of work quickly.

items: Invalid or spent transactions are refused

scenes.narration: Each full node validates blocks independently, using the same consensus rules. A node accepts a block only if all the transactions in it are valid and not already spent. So miners propose blocks, but they cannot force the network to accept an invalid one.

items: First transaction starts a new coin

scenes.narration: The first transaction in each block is a special one that starts a new coin. Transaction fees are added to the block's incentive value as well. Together, that is the block reward.
The block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks, which is about every four years. It became 3.125 bitcoin at the April 2024 halving.
And Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million coins.

items: A bigger share never decides one block

scenes.narration: Whether a particular miner finds a particular block is a matter of probability. Your chance per block is your share of the total network hashrate. A bigger share raises your odds, but it never decides any single block.
Many miners join pools. A pool shares rewards in proportion to the work each miner contributed, which smooths out payouts. Solo mining is possible, but then payouts depend on luck.

visual.caption: watts per terahash: lower is better

scenes.narration: Now the part people skip: costs. Electricity is typically a miner's largest ongoing cost, so efficiency matters. It is measured in joules per terahash, which is the same as watts per terahash, written W slash T H. Lower is more efficient.

items: Far more efficient than GPUs or CPUs
GPU mining Bitcoin is not practical

scenes.narration: That is also why mining Bitcoin with a graphics card is not practical today. Specialised chips called ASICs are far more efficient at SHA-256 than GPUs or CPUs.

scenes.text: Rewards in BTC, bills in cash

items: So results move with the price

scenes.narration: Here is another catch. Mining rewards are paid in bitcoin, but electricity and hosting are paid in regular money. So profitability moves with the bitcoin price, and returns are never certain.

items: An NFT representing a share of hashrate
Hosted in the provider's data centres
Measured in TH/s, with efficiency in W/TH

scenes.narration: Some people do not want to run hardware, so they look at services like GoMining. According to a third party explainer, GoMining sells digital miners, which are NFTs representing a share of hashrate hosted in its data centres, measured in terahash with an efficiency in watts per terahash.

items: Not redeemable for bitcoin or hardware

scenes.narration: Owners are credited daily bitcoin rewards, minus a maintenance charge that covers electricity and service costs. Digital miners are not redeemable for bitcoin, and owners do not hold the underlying hardware.

They can be low or even negative

items: Hash the header, beat the target

scenes.narration: Quick recap. Miners compete to add blocks. They hash a block header and search for a value below the target. Difficulty adjusts every 2,016 blocks. Nodes check the work. Rewards halve every 210,000 blocks, and the costs are paid in regular money.
